title: Indian Americans on the Ballot: Nine Races to Watch on Election Day
excerpt: At least 57 Indian American candidates face voters in Tuesday's midterms. Four House incumbents are favoured to return, two open-seat races will decide whether the 'Samosa Caucus' shrinks, and Vivek Ramaswamy trails narrowly in Ohio's race for governor.
body:
• At least 57 Indian American candidates are on the November 3 ballot — 1 for the Senate, 11 for the House, 3 statewide, 36 for state legislatures and 6 for local posts (IANS).
  • Four House incumbents — Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam — are rated Solid D by the Cook Political Report; Khanna and Jayapal each face an Indian American Republican challenger.
  • The House's six-member "Samosa Caucus" falls to four unless Amish Shah (Arizona) and Pia Dandiya (Florida) win their open seats.
  • Polls close Tuesday evening, state by state; the closest races — Ohio's governorship, Florida's 22nd — may not be called until Tuesday night or Wednesday.

At least 57 Indian American candidates are on the ballot in Tuesday's midterm elections, November 3 — 1 for the U.S. Senate, 11 for the House, 3 for statewide office, 36 for state legislatures and 6 for local posts, per an IANS count of candidates whose Indian heritage it could confirm.

For the community, the sharpest number is in the House. Six Indian Americans sit there now — the informal "Samosa Caucus." Two are already gone: Raja Krishnamoorthi lost the Illinois Democratic Senate primary on March 17, and Shri Thanedar lost his Michigan primary on August 4; neither is on Tuesday's ballot. The four incumbents seeking re-election are favoured to return, so whether the caucus ends the night at four, five or six rests on two open-seat races in Arizona and Florida.

The incumbents: safe seats, two all-Indian races

California's 17th District — Ro Khanna (D) vs Ritesh Tandon (R). Khanna, in Congress since 2017, is seeking a fifth term. His challenger is Ritesh Tandon, a Silicon Valley entrepreneur — one of two races here where Indian Americans face each other across party lines. No public poll exists; the Cook Political Report rates the seat Solid D.

https://x.com/TimesNow/status/2117267806718976424

Washington's 7th District — Pramila Jayapal (D) vs Nirav Sheth (R). Jayapal, the first South Asian American woman elected to Congress, is seeking a sixth term in the Seattle district. Sheth, a Gujarat-born former U.S. Marine, is the Republican nominee. No public polling exists; Cook rates the seat Solid D.

California's 3rd District — Ami Bera (D) vs Robb Tucker (R). Bera has served since 2013, longer than any other Indian American in Congress, and runs this year in the redrawn 3rd District after a decade-plus representing the neighbouring 6th. Tucker is the Republican nominee. Cook rates it Solid D; no public poll has been released.

Virginia's 10th District — Suhas Subramanyam (D) vs Dave Beckwith (R). Subramanyam, a former technology policy adviser to President Barack Obama, won this Northern Virginia seat in 2024 and is seeking a second term against Beckwith, a retired Air Force colonel. Cook rates it Solid D; no public polling is available.

The two races that decide the count

Arizona's 1st District (open) — Amish Shah (D) vs Jay Feely (R). Shah, an emergency physician and former state representative, narrowly lost this Phoenix-area seat in 2024 and is running again after Republican incumbent David Schweikert left to run for governor. Feely, a former NFL kicker, carries President Donald Trump's endorsement. The final public poll, by Keating Research (October 26–28), put Shah ahead 49 percent to 45 percent; Cook rates the race Lean D.

Florida's 22nd District (open) — Pia Dandiya (D) vs Casey Askar (R). Dandiya, a former teacher and principal who served as a White House fellow, is the Democratic nominee in this redrawn Palm Beach County seat, whose new lines voted for Trump by 10 points in 2024. Askar is a Naples businessman. Cook rates it a Toss-up; Sabato's Crystal Ball moved it to Leans D in its final ratings. The only public polling comes from a Democratic-aligned sponsor and shows a statistical tie — RedBox Research (October 20–23) had Dandiya at 46.3 percent and Askar at 45.5 percent — so the numbers deserve caution. Wins for both Shah and Dandiya would hold the caucus at six.

"The House's six-member "Samosa Caucus" falls to four unless Amish Shah (Arizona) and Pia Dandiya (Florida) win their open seats."

Statewide: Ohio's governor and New York's attorney general

Ohio governor (open) — Vivek Ramaswamy (R) vs Amy Acton (D). The most closely watched race on this list. Ramaswamy, the Cincinnati-born businessman and former presidential candidate, is the Republican nominee for governor; Acton is the Democratic nominee. The final New York Times/Siena College poll (October 26 to November 1) put Acton ahead 49 percent to 43 percent, while a final Emerson College poll had the two tied at 48 percent each. Acton leads narrowly in the closing polling averages, and Cook rates the race Lean D.

New York attorney general — Saritha Komatireddy (R) vs Letitia James (D). Komatireddy, a former federal prosecutor, is challenging James, the Democratic incumbent. The latest independent polling, by Siena College (October 19–22), gave James 54 percent to Komatireddy's 39 percent.

The long shot

Ohio's 13th District — Sandeep Dixit (independent). Dixit, an engineer and small-business owner, is running without a party in a three-way race against the Democratic incumbent, Emilia Sykes, and the Republican nominee, Carey Coleman. No public polling exists; Cook rates the seat Likely D.

Polls close Tuesday evening, state by state, and first results arrive Tuesday night; the closest races — Ohio's governorship, Arizona's 1st and Florida's 22nd — may not be called until Wednesday. Our state-by-state guide to when winners are announced has the timings; our earlier analysis sets out what is at stake in the House count.
